claim: Probability-format Bayesian problems are solved by few humans (about 4 to 16 percent); natural frequencies raise this to about 24 to 50 percent but not to ceiling. Format helps, does not fix.
agent_test: Run the same base-rate items in probability vs natural-frequency format on the agent at equal tokens; score exact posterior.
audit_note: Gigerenzer and Hoffrage: Bayesian algorithms 16% (standard probability) and 28% (short) vs 46%/50% frequencies; the 4% vs 24% pair is McDowell and Jacobs (2017) meta-analysis as reported by Weber et al. 2018 (second-hand); range 4-16 skips the 28% short-probability cell. Minor.

claim: Legal professionals and law students fail source/guilt inference on a DNA match in probability format (13 percent and under 1 percent correct) and do much better with natural frequencies (68 and 44 percent).
agent_test: Replicate the Hoffrage DNA case with the LLM in both formats; compare to the human numbers.

claim: Converting evidence to counts of cases out of N before reasoning is a cheap, code-checkable step that matches what helps humans.
agent_test: Add a convert-to-counts step; measure accuracy gain vs plain chain-of-thought at equal tokens.
audit_note: Natural-frequency format helps humans (Gigerenzer and Hoffrage 16 to 46-50%; Weber 4 to 24%; exposure study) so 'matches what helps humans' holds; 'cheap, code-checkable' is the author's engineering judgement, not sourced, and the cited gains leave most people still failing.

claim: Many people given natural frequencies still calculate with probabilities (49 percent), and few translate probabilities into frequencies (18 percent): the format is not self-applying.
agent_test: Test whether the agent self-translates when given probability text, versus when told to.

claim: Brief training (tree or formula) lifts human Bayesian accuracy to about 86-89 percent, with decay at one month (about 68-72 percent); repeated exposure rivals lightweight training.
agent_test: Few-shot worked examples in the prompt vs none; measure transfer to new base-rate problems.
audit: downgraded 2026-11-20 by check_established.py: only 1 opened source(s) from distinct authors

claim: Prosecutor's fallacy (confusing P(E|H) with P(H|E)) is formally resolved by prior odds times likelihood ratio: LR 1,000 with prior 1:9,999 gives posterior near 9 percent source.
agent_test: Ask agent to state both conditionals explicitly and compute odds form; verify arithmetic by script.
audit_note: Fenton, Neil and Berger give prior 1/10,000 to posterior 9% with LR 1000 (1000/9999 = about 9.1%); Cuellar's abstract only recommends reporting LRs, not the worked arithmetic.

claim: Sally Clark: the 1 in 73 million figure (1/8,543 squared) assumed independence and ignored the competing-hypothesis comparison; after one SIDS death the second is 6-10 times likelier; Hill estimated odds 4.5:1 to 9:1.
agent_test: Give the agent the Clark statistics and check it names the independence assumption and the alternative hypothesis.
audit_note: Feeny and Stamboulid says Hill found 6-10 times; Wikipedia says dependency factor 5-10 (small source disagreement); odds 4.5:1 to 9:1 are double SIDS vs double homicide, which the claim leaves unspecified.

claim: Fenton argues that failing to define exclusive and exhaustive hypotheses may itself have exaggerated the Bayesian critique of Clark: reanalyses are model-dependent.
agent_test: Require the agent to list the hypothesis set and check exclusivity before a posterior.

claim: Mock jurors revise beliefs in the correct direction but not by Bayesian computation (Shengelia and Lagnado 2021); earlier work reports conservative updating that grows with the amount of evidence (Schum 1966), and in Martire et al. belief change was over 350,000 times smaller than the expert intended (reported in a literature review).
agent_test: Elicit stepwise posteriors from the agent and compare with a Bayesian-network reference; test for conservatism.
audit_note: Shengelia and Lagnado's own result is that mock jurors revised beliefs in the right direction but without exact Bayesian computation and with errors in weighting evidence; conservatism and a gap growing with evidence amount are cited background (Phillips and Edwards, Schum 1966), not their finding; the 350,000-times figure is Martire et al. as reported second-hand in a review.
claim_before_audit: Mock jurors are poor intuitive Bayesians: conservative updating, with the gap growing with the amount of evidence; belief change was reported far smaller than experts intended.

claim: The format of forensic conclusion (LR, random match probability, verbal, categorical) made no detectable difference to mock-juror evidence weight (Exp 1 F=.10, Exp 2 F=.26) or verdict; numeracy and comprehension mattered.
agent_test: Not an agent test; informs how the agent presents results to humans: do not rely on format alone.
audit_note: Martire et al. 2025 stats verified (Exp1 F(3,442)=.102, Exp2 F(2,310)=.255, verdict chi-square ns); Exp 1 had four formats and Exp 2 three, so the four-format list applies to Exp 1 only (minor); review supports with Thompson and Newman.

claim: A weak evidence effect exists: weak inculpatory evidence can lower belief in guilt, mostly with verbal expressions.
agent_test: Feed weak inculpatory evidence and check the agent never moves belief the wrong way.

claim: Professionals do not reliably detect unsound forensic reports: only 32 percent rated the unsound report unreliable; reliability ratings 3.3 vs 3.1 not different.
agent_test: Test whether the agent flags a methodologically flawed report at equal tokens.

claim: Clinicians and students score poorly on confidence-weighted Bayesian items (65 to 93 percent wrong; negative confidence-weighted scores); expertise and cognitive reflection help.
agent_test: Compare accuracy and stated confidence of the agent on the same items; measure calibration.
audit: downgraded 2026-11-20 by check_established.py: only 1 opened source(s) from distinct authors

claim: Frontier LLMs can match or beat typical humans on classic base-rate vignettes (o1 100 percent correct; ChatGPT-4 96 percent on CRT) but remain sensitive to wording and context. Base-rate neglect with vivid descriptions is strong in 2024 models (odds ratio about 1.2 instead of 9, Li and Rui); GPT-5 still makes a conjunction fallacy in 18.8 percent of judgments vs 58.5 percent for humans.
agent_test: Run a perturbed base-rate battery (swap names, numbers, framing) and measure accuracy drop.
audit_note: Verified: o1 100% base-rate item (vignette study), ChatGPT-4 96% on CRT (Hagendorff), Li and Rui odds ratios 1.25/1.18 vs normative 9, GPT-5 conjunction fallacy 18.8% vs 58.5% humans; the 96% CRT figure is the fraction of correct answers for ChatGPT-4 and the o1 100% is on one vignette scenario.

claim: LLM probability judgments show dual traits: posterior tracks similarity (Pearson 0.90-0.98) and the same model gives different priors alone vs inside a judgment.
agent_test: Elicit prior alone and prior inside posterior; flag inconsistency by script.
audit_note: Numbers verified (Pearson 0.90-0.98; GPT-4o prior 2-4% alone vs 10-30% in judgment) but every specific figure comes from one paper (Li and Rui 2024); Jiang et al. concerns token bias in conjunction and syllogism tasks and does not test this finding.

claim: Chain-of-thought alone does not fix probabilistic reasoning: Bayesian teaching beat CoT variants; CoT accuracy on Bayesian networks collapses with network size (GPT-4 zero-shot 79 percent at 2 variables, 27 at 4, 6-17 above). Gap 4 closed for 2024 models: GPT-4 few-shot CoT row is 78, 64, 36, 25, 22, 16, 7, 7, 7 (V2 to V10); 2025-2026 reasoning models still untested.
agent_test: At equal tokens compare plain CoT versus CoT with tool-computed posterior on growing evidence chains.
audit_note: Nafar et al. rows match (zero-shot 79,63,27,10,17,6,5,7,6; few-shot 78,64,36,25,22,16,7,7,7); the largest-network zero-shot values go down to 5, not 6; Qiu et al. tested CoT on flight-recommendation, not Bayesian networks, so 'beat CoT variants' is across different tasks.

claim: Offloading inference to a probabilistic solver restores accuracy: in BLInD, GPT-4 with ProbLog stays 96-100% on 2-10 variable networks while plain Python (PAL) falls to 7-10%; in an exploratory study Keppens (2026) found 100% correct LR explanations once the LLM is told to use solver-supplied marginals and LRs rather than recompute them. BLInD states numbers and links outright (GPT-4 number extraction 100%), so it tests translation, not elicitation of structure.
agent_test: Offload posterior arithmetic to a solver tool vs in-head; compare error rate at equal tokens.
audit_note: Nafar numbers verified (ProbLog 96-100 for GPT-4; PAL 7 at V10, 10 with number extraction; number extraction 100%), but Keppens' 100% is correct explanations of Bayesian-network-derived LRs when the LLM is told not to recompute the supplied LR, an exploratory workshop study, not LLM accuracy on computing LRs.
claim_before_audit: Offloading inference to a probabilistic solver or code restores accuracy: ProbLog stays 96-100 percent for GPT-4 on 2-10 variable nets, Keppens' hybrid was 100 percent correct on LRs; plain Python (PAL) fell to 7-10 percent. Caveat from the BLInD design: numbers and links are stated outright in the text (GPT-4 number extraction 100 percent), so this tests translation, not elicitation of structure.

claim: Unconstrained LLM explanations of Bayesian-network LRs can be wrong and then rationalised: one network gave 390.4 vs correct 18.07 (about 21 times too high); 4 of 100 runs wrong on another.
agent_test: Check agent likelihood-ratio statements against a symbolic calculation on small networks.

claim: Bayesian teaching fine-tuning gives about 80 percent agreement with a Bayesian assistant on held-out tasks across three 7-9B models, generalising to other domains.
agent_test: Out of scope for a scaffold (training). Compare to scaffold gains on a small model.

claim: Prompt-level Bayesian instructions can hurt forecasting: the Bayesian Reasoning prompt raised Brier by 0.03 (worse); Base Rate First helped slightly (about 0.011-0.016).
agent_test: Equal-token comparison of base-rate-first vs Bayesian-reasoning prompt on resolved questions.

claim: LLMs show belief entrenchment: Martingale Scores positive in 51 of 54 CoT setups; a score of 0.04 already makes forecasts worse than chance Brier 0.25. Related: GPT-4o under-updates relative to Bayes computed from its own priors and likelihood ratios (Qiao et al. 2026, Sally-Clark-style vignette).
agent_test: Compute the Martingale Score of the agent's belief updates; check that updates are not predictable from the prior.

claim: Forewarning an LLM about cognitive biases changes style more than substance: bias named correctly in only 5 percent, average bias reduction 6.9 percent, though some biases moved (framing 66 to 45 percent). Generic role or carefulness prompts (legal expert, meticulous, justify) gave limited, inconsistent reduction of order bias in GPT-4o and GPT-5.2 (Bessis et al. 2026). Specific hypothesis-listing was not tested.
agent_test: Compare a generic warning against a specific operator step for a named bias.

claim: Legal-doctrine critics argue LRs have no place in criminal trials and that probabilistic reporting faces practical obstacles; the debate is unresolved.
agent_test: None for the agent; flag when output is for legal use.

claim: Evidence order changes GPT-4o's legal judgments: on a murder vignette (Qiao et al. 2026 preprint) mean final guilt was 0.66 with the defence evidence first vs 0.40 with it last, guilty verdicts were virtually eliminated when defence evidence came last (OR 0.002), and step-by-step judging raised guilty-verdict odds 10.55-fold. In Bessis et al. (2026, 1-10 guilt scale, double-rating baseline) GPT-5.2 shows the same direction but weaker (4.75 vs 5.35) than GPT-4o (4.24 vs 6.04).
agent_test: Run the same evidence set in two or more orders and accumulate log-odds in code; flag the case if the verdict flips.
audit_note: All numbers verified (Qiao: 0.66 vs 0.40, OR 0.002, SbS OR 10.55; Bessis: GPT-5.2 4.75 vs 5.35, GPT-4o 4.24 vs 6.04 in the double-rating baseline), but Qiao's case is a generic murder vignette, not described as Sally-Clark-style; Bessis' means are on a different 1-10 scale in one rating condition.
claim_before_audit: Evidence order changes LLM legal judgments: GPT-4o final guilt 0.66 (defence first) vs 0.40 (defence last) on a Sally-Clark-style case, almost no guilty verdicts when defence evidence comes last (OR 0.002); step-by-step judging raised guilty-verdict odds 10.5-fold. GPT-5.2 shows the same direction but weaker (means 4.75 vs 5.35 against GPT-4o 4.24 vs 6.04).

claim: Frontier LLMs are conservative Bayesians on legal evidence: stated guilt moves the right way but less than Bayes computed from the model's own priors and likelihood ratios, for all role framings and both response modes (GPT-4o only; reasoning models not yet tested).
agent_test: Elicit LRs only, multiply in code, and compare to the model's own stated posterior.

claim: Generic prompts (legal expert, meticulous, justify, forewarn) do not reliably remove LLM bias in legal-style tasks; whether explicit hypothesis listing helps on Sally-Clark-type dependent evidence is untested.
agent_test: A/B: generic warning vs listing H1 and H2 plus stating dependence between evidence items, on a dependent-evidence battery.

claim: LLMs map verbal probability words to numbers inconsistently and closer to lay readings than guidance (for 'common', 16.5 to 65.5 percent across four chatbots vs EC 1-10 percent); they often decline to give a number (31 to 94 percent abstention).
agent_test: Calibrate each model's verbal scale against numeric LRs before using verbal strengths.

claim: Koehler (1996) argues base rates are generally used by people, more so with frequencies and reliable rates, and that a mechanical base-rate-fallacy label is normatively wrong when assumptions are unchecked; this competes with the neglect narrative. Thompson and Schumann (1987) experimental numbers remain unverified.
agent_test: Check the reliability and reference class of a base rate before applying it.

claim: Told to use natural frequencies, reasoning LLMs apply the format partially or inconsistently (o3-mini correct, Gemini relabelled only, DeepSeek R1 reverted and erred in one run); no controlled equal-token test of a convert-to-counts operator exists in the sources found.
agent_test: Build the convert-to-counts operator with a checker (counts sum to N) and test on a perturbed battery.

claim: No source found measures LLM commission of the prosecutor's fallacy on realistic forensic prose, re-runs the Hoffrage DNA problem with LLMs or legal professionals (2020-2026), or tests LLM readers on forensic conclusion format; these are open experiments.
agent_test: Own harness: 30 forensic summaries with seeded transposed conditionals; measure detection and commission rates.
